title: Facial Expressions in Adolescent-Parent Interactions and Links with Anxiety and Depression: A Dyadic Approach
abstract: Close relationships play a key role in mental health, and facial expressions are important social signals in our interactions. Few studies have examined facial expressions of emotion and links with anxiety and depression in adolescent-parent interactions, which may be crucibles for mental health development. Drawing from affective, developmental, and clinical science frameworks, the present laboratory-based study used a dyadic approach to examine facial expressions of emotion (objectively measured on a frame-by-frame basis) during conflict, pleasant, and neutral adolescent-parent interactions (each lasting 10 minutes) and links with anxiety and depressive symptoms (each measured in both adolescents and parents). A total of 2,490,000 video frames across 1,660 video minutes in 28 adolescent-parent dyads were analyzed using actor-partner interdependence modeling. Results revealed that (a) adolescents’ neutral expressions were positively associated with adolescents’ and parents’ anxiety and depression, (b) parents’ negative expressions were positively associated with adolescents’ and parents’ anxiety and depression, and (c) adolescents’ happy expressions were negatively associated with parents’ anxiety and depression (although this association was not robust when controlling for demographic variables). Results largely generalized across the three interaction contexts (conflict, pleasant, and neutral). Together, these results suggest the utility of facial expressions (neutral expressions for adolescents, negative expressions for parents) as behavioral markers of psychopathology, emphasize the importance of adolescent-parent interactions for anxiety and depression, and suggest directions for future affective, developmental, and clinical research.
